course.title: Deep Learning
course.description: Deep learning is the branch of machine learning that builds layered neural networks able to learn useful patterns straight from raw data. This course walks from a single artificial neuron up through feedforward, convolutional, recurrent, and transformer networks, explaining how they train, where they fail, and what it takes to use them responsibly. Scope and structure adapted from the Deep learning article on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between deep learning and machine learning?
options: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that uses layered neural networks
Machine learning is a subset of deep learning
They are two names for one algorithm
questions.explanation: Deep learning is a part of machine learning, set apart by its use of many-layered neural networks.

questions.prompt: An artificial neuron produces its output by...
options: taking a weighted sum of inputs, adding a bias, then applying an activation function
questions.explanation: A neuron computes z = w1*x1 + ... + wn*xn + b, then passes z through an activation function.

options: the input unchanged for every value
zero for negative inputs and the input itself for positive inputs
questions.explanation: relu(z) = max(0, z): it zeroes out negatives and leaves positives alone.

questions.prompt: Gradient descent improves a model by...
options: moving weights in the direction that increases the loss
moving weights a small step opposite to the gradient of the loss
choosing fresh random weights each step
questions.explanation: The gradient points uphill, so you step the other way to make the loss smaller.

options: does poorly on both training and new data
fits the training data closely but fails to generalize to new data
has too few parameters to learn anything
questions.explanation: An overfit model has memorized quirks of the training set that do not carry over to unseen data.

questions.prompt: A convolutional neural network is especially suited to...
questions.explanation: Convolution exploits local structure in grids, which is exactly how pixels are arranged.

questions.prompt: The transformer architecture relies mainly on...
options: an attention mechanism that relates different positions in a sequence
questions.explanation: Attention lets each position look at every other position and weigh what matters.

questions.prompt: A train / validation / test split exists so that...
options: the model sees the same data three times
you tune choices on validation data and judge final quality on untouched test data
questions.explanation: Keeping the test set untouched gives an honest estimate of performance on new data.

lessons.title: What deep learning is
lessons.grammar_note: Deep learning, machine learning, and artificial intelligence are nested ideas, not synonyms - deep learning sits inside machine learning, which sits inside artificial intelligence.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to place deep learning inside the wider field of machine learning, explain what the word 'deep' actually refers to, and say in plain terms why layered networks can learn features that older methods had to be handed by people. Warm-up from the diagnostic: is deep learning a subset of machine learning, or is it the other way around? Hold on to that answer, because the whole course is built on it. You will also be able to describe the kind of problem deep learning is good at - finding patterns in large amounts of raw data such as images, sound, and text - and the kind it struggles with, such as tasks with very little data or where every decision must be fully explained. Treat this lesson as the map you will keep returning to. Every later topic, from a single neuron to a full transformer, is just one more region drawn in on that map, so a clear overview now pays off in every lesson that follows.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Machine learning is the practice of writing programs that get better at a task by learning from data, instead of following step-by-step rules a person wrote by hand. Deep learning is one family inside machine learning. What makes it 'deep' is that it stacks many layers of simple computing units, called neurons, one after another. Each layer transforms the data a little and passes it along, so early layers in an image network might detect edges, middle layers combine edges into shapes, and later layers assemble shapes into whole objects. The central difference from older machine learning is representation learning: rather than a person deciding which features of the data matter, the network discovers useful features on its own while training. That is why deep learning has done so well on messy, high-dimensional inputs like photographs and raw audio. The trade-off is that it usually needs large datasets and heavy computation. Artificial intelligence is the broadest of the three terms - it names the whole goal of making machines act intelligently - and machine learning, with deep learning inside it, is the approach driving most current progress toward that goal.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: Consider telling cats from dogs in photographs. A classic machine learning approach needs a person to design measurements - ear shape, fur texture, snout length - and feed those numbers to a classifier. A deep learning approach instead feeds the raw pixels to a network and lets it learn its own internal measurements, layer by layer. A second example: predicting the next word in a sentence. Older systems counted word pairs by hand, while a deep network reads millions of sentences and builds a rich internal sense of how words relate. The general recipe is always the same three parts. First, a model: a network holding many adjustable numbers called weights. Second, a loss: a single number that says how wrong the current guesses are. Third, an optimizer: a procedure that nudges the weights to make the loss smaller. You will meet each part in detail later. For now, notice the pattern - define a model, measure its error, improve it - because every deep learning system, however large, is that same loop repeated many times across a great deal of data.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Write your answers before reading on, since recalling is stronger practice than recognizing. 1) In one sentence, how does deep learning differ from older machine learning? 2) What does the word 'deep' describe? 3) Name one data type deep learning handles well and one situation where it struggles. 4) Put these three terms from broadest to narrowest: machine learning, deep learning, artificial intelligence. 5) What are the three parts of every deep learning system? 6) True or false: the network is handed the right features to use. Answers: 1) Deep learning learns its own features from raw data using many layers, rather than relying on features a person designs. 2) The number of stacked layers in the network. 3) It handles images, audio, and text well; it struggles when data is scarce or when every decision must be fully explained. 4) Artificial intelligence, then machine learning, then deep learning. 5) A model with weights, a loss that measures error, and an optimizer that reduces the loss. 6) False - it discovers them during training.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating deep learning, machine learning, and artificial intelligence as interchangeable words - they are nested, with deep learning the most specific of the three. Mistake: assuming deep learning is always the right tool; when you have only a few hundred examples, simpler methods often win and are far easier to explain. Mistake: believing the network is given the correct features to look at - it discovers them, which is both its great strength and the reason its decisions can be hard to interpret. Mistake: picturing 'deep' as something mysterious rather than literally many layers. Exit ticket: (a) Is deep learning a subset of machine learning, or the reverse? (b) What is 'representation learning' in one short phrase? Answers: deep learning is a subset of machine learning; representation learning is the network learning useful features from raw data by itself, instead of being handed features that a person designed in advance.

lessons.title: The artificial neuron and activation functions
lessons.grammar_note: Without a nonlinear activation, stacking layers gains you nothing - a chain of linear steps is still just one linear step.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to describe the single artificial neuron that every deep network is built from, write out the weighted sum it computes using plain-ASCII notation, and explain why an activation function is applied on top of that sum. You will be able to contrast two of the most common activations - the sigmoid and the ReLU - and say when each tends to be used. Warm-up from the diagnostic: in words, what are the two steps a neuron performs on its inputs? Keep that in mind as we make it precise. You will also be able to explain, in one sentence, why networks need a nonlinear activation at all, which is one of the most important ideas in the whole course. Once a single neuron is clear, a layer is just many neurons working side by side, and a deep network is just many such layers, so the small object you learn here scales all the way up to the largest models you will meet later.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An artificial neuron takes several input numbers and combines them in two steps. First it forms a weighted sum: z = w1*x1 + w2*x2 + ... + wn*xn + b, where each weight wi says how much input xi matters and b is a bias that shifts the result. Second, it passes z through an activation function to produce the neuron's output. The activation is where nonlinearity enters, and that matters enormously: if every neuron were purely linear, stacking many layers would collapse into a single linear transformation, and the network could never model curved or complex relationships. The sigmoid activation, sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(-z)), squeezes any number into the range 0 to 1, which is handy for probabilities but can slow learning when z is large in size because its slope flattens out. The ReLU activation, relu(z) = max(0, z), simply zeroes negatives and keeps positives. It is cheap to compute and keeps a healthy slope for positive inputs, which is why it became the default hidden-layer activation in most modern networks.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: Work a neuron by hand. Suppose a neuron has weights w1 = 0.5 and w2 = -1.0, bias b = 0.2, and inputs x1 = 4, x2 = 1. Then z = 0.5*4 + (-1.0)*1 + 0.2 = 2.0 - 1.0 + 0.2 = 1.2. With a ReLU activation the output is max(0, 1.2) = 1.2. With a sigmoid the output is 1 / (1 + e^(-1.2)), which is about 0.77. Now flip x1 to -4: z = 0.5*(-4) - 1.0*1 + 0.2 = -2.8. ReLU gives max(0, -2.8) = 0, so the neuron stays silent, while sigmoid gives about 0.06, a small but nonzero value. This shows the key contrast: ReLU can switch a neuron fully off, which helps networks build sparse, specialized responses, whereas sigmoid always lets a little signal through. In a real layer you would have many neurons, each with its own weights and bias, all reading the same inputs and each producing one output number that the next layer will read in turn.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Compute each by hand and check yourself. 1) A neuron has w1 = 2, w2 = 3, b = -1, inputs x1 = 1, x2 = 1. Find z. 2) Apply ReLU to that z. 3) What does ReLU return for z = -5? 4) What range does sigmoid always land in? 5) In one sentence, why do networks need a nonlinear activation? 6) Which activation can switch a neuron completely off? Answers: 1) z = 2*1 + 3*1 - 1 = 4. 2) relu(4) = max(0, 4) = 4. 3) relu(-5) = max(0, -5) = 0. 4) Between 0 and 1. 5) Without nonlinearity a stack of layers collapses into one linear map, so the network could only model straight-line relationships. 6) ReLU, since it outputs exactly 0 for any negative input while sigmoid never quite reaches 0.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: forgetting the bias term b, which lets a neuron shift its threshold and is as important as the weights. Mistake: thinking more layers alone add power - without a nonlinear activation between them, extra linear layers add nothing. Mistake: assuming sigmoid is always best because it looks smooth; its flat tails make large networks learn slowly, which is a big reason ReLU took over for hidden layers. Mistake: reading relu(z) = max(0, z) as rounding rather than as clipping negatives to zero. Exit ticket: (a) Write the weighted sum a neuron computes in plain-ASCII form. (b) Why is a nonlinear activation necessary? Answers: z = w1*x1 + w2*x2 + ... + wn*xn + b; the nonlinearity is what keeps a deep stack from collapsing into a single linear function, so the network can represent curved and complex patterns rather than only straight-line ones.

lessons.title: Feedforward networks and layers
lessons.grammar_note: In a feedforward network, information flows one way - input to output - with no loops back; layers between the input and output are called hidden layers.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to describe a feedforward neural network as a stack of layers, explain what input, hidden, and output layers each do, and count the weights that connect two fully connected layers. Warm-up from the diagnostic and the last lesson: a layer is just many neurons side by side - so if one neuron reads all the inputs, what does a layer of five neurons produce? You will be able to explain why depth, meaning more hidden layers, lets a network build features in stages, and why width, meaning more neurons per layer, lets each stage hold more detail. You will also be able to read a simple network diagram and say how an input vector is transformed step by step into an output. This lesson connects the single neuron you just studied to the full networks you will train later, so by the end the phrase 'a three-layer network' should call up a concrete picture rather than a vague one.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A feedforward network arranges neurons in layers and sends information in one direction only: from the input layer, through one or more hidden layers, to the output layer, with no connections looping backward. The input layer is just the raw numbers you feed in - for a small grayscale image, one value per pixel. Each hidden layer is a set of neurons that each read every output of the previous layer, compute their weighted sums and activations, and pass their outputs forward. This full connection is why such layers are called 'dense' or 'fully connected'. The output layer produces the final answer: a single number for a simple prediction, or several numbers, one per class, for classification. Depth refers to how many layers are stacked, and it is what lets the network learn features in stages - simple parts first, richer combinations later. Width refers to how many neurons sit in a layer, which controls how much a single stage can represent. A deep, suitably wide network can approximate very complicated input-to-output relationships, which is the whole reason the architecture is so flexible.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: Count the connections, because that is where the learning lives. Suppose an input layer has 3 values feeding a hidden layer of 4 neurons. Each of the 4 neurons has one weight per input, so that is 4*3 = 12 weights, plus 4 biases, one per neuron. If that hidden layer then feeds an output layer of 2 neurons, that adds 4*2 = 8 more weights and 2 biases. The whole tiny network therefore holds 12 + 8 = 20 weights and 6 biases - 26 adjustable numbers in all, and training is the process of setting them well. Now trace a forward pass. The 3 input numbers enter; the hidden layer turns them into 4 activation values; the output layer turns those 4 values into 2 final numbers. Every arrow in a diagram is one weight being multiplied, and every neuron is one weighted sum followed by an activation. Scale this picture up - thousands of inputs, several hidden layers, hundreds of neurons each - and you have the kind of network used in practice, built entirely from the small pieces shown here.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Work these out and check yourself. 1) In a feedforward network, which direction does information flow? 2) What is a hidden layer? 3) An input of 5 values feeds a hidden layer of 10 neurons; how many weights connect them, ignoring biases? 4) How many biases does that hidden layer have? 5) What does adding more hidden layers give a network? 6) What does a fully connected layer mean? Answers: 1) One way, from input toward output, with no loops back. 2) Any layer of neurons between the input and the output layers. 3) 10*5 = 50 weights. 4) 10 biases, one per neuron. 5) More depth, which lets it build features in stages, from simple parts to richer combinations. 6) A layer in which every neuron reads every output of the previous layer.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: counting layers inconsistently - a common convention counts the hidden and output layers but not the raw input layer, so agree on a convention before you argue about depth. Mistake: forgetting the biases when counting parameters; each neuron has exactly one. Mistake: assuming wider always beats deeper or the reverse - depth stages features while width widens each stage, and good networks balance both. Mistake: imagining the hidden layers hold human-readable concepts; they usually hold useful but hard-to-name combinations. Exit ticket: (a) Between an input layer of 4 and a hidden layer of 6, how many weights are there? (b) What makes a network 'deep' rather than shallow? Answers: 6*4 = 24 weights; a network is called deep when it has several hidden layers stacked between input and output, rather than just one.

lessons.title: How networks learn: loss, gradient descent, and backpropagation
lessons.grammar_note: Training is a loop: make predictions, measure the loss, compute gradients by backpropagation, then take a gradient-descent step - repeat.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain, conceptually, how a network actually learns: how a loss function scores its mistakes, how gradient descent reduces that score, and what backpropagation computes so the step can be taken. Warm-up from the diagnostic: gradient descent moves the weights in which direction relative to the gradient of the loss? You will be able to describe the training loop in order, write the weight-update rule in plain-ASCII form, and say in one sentence what the learning rate controls. You will also be able to explain, without the heavy calculus, why backpropagation is just the chain rule applied layer by layer, working backward from the output. This is the heart of the whole course - every network, however large, learns by this same loop - so the goal is a clear mental model rather than a full derivation. By the end you should be able to narrate what happens to the weights across one training step from start to finish.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Learning starts with a loss function, a single number measuring how wrong the network's current predictions are across the training data. For predicting a continuous value, a common loss is mean squared error: L = (1/N) * sum((y_pred - y_true)^2), which grows as guesses drift from the truth. For classification, cross-entropy is used, which is large when the network is confidently wrong. Training then tries to make L as small as possible by adjusting the weights. The tool is gradient descent. The gradient of the loss is the direction in weight-space that increases L fastest, so you step the opposite way: w := w - learning_rate * gradient, applied to every weight. The learning rate is a small positive number setting the step size - too large and training overshoots and diverges, too small and it crawls. Backpropagation is how the gradient for every weight is found efficiently. Starting from the loss at the output, it applies the chain rule layer by layer back toward the input, reusing the computations from the forward pass, so even a network with millions of weights can be updated in one backward sweep.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: Picture the loss as a landscape of hills and valleys, with each weight one axis of position and height equal to L. Gradient descent is like walking downhill in fog: you feel the slope under your feet - that is the gradient - and step the steepest way down. A concrete mini-step: suppose one weight w = 0.80, the gradient of the loss with respect to w is +2.0, and the learning rate is 0.1. Then w := 0.80 - 0.1*2.0 = 0.60, nudging w down because increasing it would have raised the loss. Repeat this for every weight, every batch of data, many times over, and the loss trends downward. In practice you rarely use the whole dataset per step; you use a small random batch, which is called stochastic or mini-batch gradient descent and is both faster and noisier. One full pass over the training data is called an epoch, and training usually runs for many epochs. Backpropagation quietly supplies the gradient for each weight at every step, which is what makes this scale to large networks.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Work these and check yourself. 1) What does a loss function measure? 2) In the rule w := w - learning_rate * gradient, which way does w move relative to the gradient? 3) A weight is 1.0, its gradient is +4.0, and the learning rate is 0.25; what is the new weight? 4) What does the learning rate control? 5) What does backpropagation compute? 6) What is one epoch? Answers: 1) How wrong the network's current predictions are, as a single number. 2) Opposite to the gradient, since the gradient points uphill and we want to go down. 3) 1.0 - 0.25*4.0 = 0.0. 4) The size of each gradient-descent step. 5) The gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, found by the chain rule working backward from the output. 6) One full pass over the entire training dataset.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: stepping in the direction of the gradient rather than against it, which would increase the loss instead of lowering it. Mistake: setting the learning rate too high, so the loss bounces around or blows up, or too low, so training barely moves - picking it well is one of the first things to tune. Mistake: thinking backpropagation is a separate kind of learning; it is only the efficient way to get the gradients that gradient descent then uses. Mistake: expecting the loss to drop smoothly every single step - with mini-batches it wiggles down, and that is normal. Exit ticket: (a) Write the weight-update rule in plain-ASCII form. (b) In one sentence, what is backpropagation? Answers: w := w - learning_rate * gradient; backpropagation is applying the chain rule layer by layer, backward from the loss, to compute how much each weight contributed to the error so gradient descent knows how to adjust it.

options: a person designs the features by hand
the network discovers useful features from raw data on its own
the data is stored in a database
the model is drawn as a diagram
questions.explanation: Learning its own features from raw data is what sets deep learning apart from older methods.

questions.prompt: A neuron computes z = w1*x1 + w2*x2 + b with w1 = 1, w2 = 2, b = 0, x1 = 3, x2 = 1. What is z?
The sigmoid function always outputs a value...
questions.explanation: sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(-z)) is squeezed into the open range 0 to 1.

questions.prompt: Why do hidden layers need a nonlinear activation?
options: because otherwise stacked layers collapse into a single linear map
questions.explanation: Without nonlinearity, any number of linear layers is equivalent to just one.

questions.prompt: Gradient descent updates a weight using which rule?
questions.explanation: You step opposite the gradient, scaled by the learning rate, to lower the loss.

lessons.title: Generalization: overfitting, regularization, dropout, and data splits
lessons.grammar_note: The goal is never low training error for its own sake - it is low error on new, unseen data, which is called generalization.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to tell overfitting from underfitting, explain why a train / validation / test split is the standard way to measure honest performance, and describe two everyday cures for overfitting: regularization and dropout. Warm-up from the diagnostic: what does overfitting look like in terms of training error versus error on new data? You will be able to say which split you tune choices on and which split you must leave untouched until the very end, and why mixing those up quietly fools you into thinking a model is better than it is. You will also be able to explain, in plain terms, what dropout does during training and why randomly ignoring neurons makes a network more robust. This lesson is where many real projects succeed or fail, because a model that scores well only on data it has already seen is worth very little, and the habits here are what keep you honest.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A model generalizes when it performs well on data it has never seen. Two failures block this. Underfitting is when the model is too simple or undertrained and does poorly even on the training data. Overfitting is the opposite: the model fits the training data closely, even its noise and quirks, but then stumbles on new data. To detect this, you split your data into three parts. The training set is what the network learns from. The validation set is used to tune choices - how many layers, which learning rate, when to stop - without touching the final judge. The test set is locked away and used only once, at the end, to estimate real-world performance. Regularization fights overfitting by discouraging overly large weights; a common form adds a penalty on weight size to the loss, nudging the network toward simpler solutions. Dropout is a second technique: during each training step it randomly switches off a fraction of neurons, so the network cannot lean on any single unit and must spread what it learns, which tends to generalize better.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: Suppose you train a network and see training accuracy of 99 percent but validation accuracy of 70 percent. That large gap is the signature of overfitting: the model has memorized the training set. Several fixes apply. Get more data if you can, since more examples make memorizing harder. Add regularization so the loss becomes L = error + lambda * (size of the weights), where lambda sets how strongly large weights are penalized. Add dropout, say dropping 20 percent of neurons at random each step during training, then using the full network at test time. Use early stopping: watch validation error and stop training once it starts rising even as training error keeps falling. A worked habit: a dataset of 10000 examples might be split 8000 for training, 1000 for validation, and 1000 for test. You would try several settings, compare them only on the validation set, pick the best, and finally - exactly once - report its number on the test set. If you peek at the test set to make choices, that number stops being trustworthy.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer and check yourself. 1) What is overfitting in one sentence? 2) Which of the three splits do you tune choices on? 3) Which split must stay untouched until the very end? 4) What does dropout do during training? 5) What does early stopping watch to decide when to stop? 6) You see 98 percent training accuracy and 72 percent validation accuracy - what is the likely problem? Answers: 1) The model fits the training data, including its noise, but fails to generalize to new data. 2) The validation set. 3) The test set. 4) It randomly switches off a fraction of neurons so the network cannot depend on any single one. 5) The validation error, stopping once it starts to rise. 6) Overfitting, shown by the large gap between training and validation scores.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: tuning your choices on the test set, which turns the final honest number into an optimistic lie - use the validation set for all decisions. Mistake: leaving dropout switched on at test time; dropout is a training-only trick, and you evaluate with the full network. Mistake: reading low training error as success, when the only score that matters is error on new data. Mistake: adding so much regularization that the model can no longer fit even the training data, which swaps overfitting for underfitting. Exit ticket: (a) Which data split gives the honest final estimate of performance? (b) In one sentence, how does dropout help? Answers: the test set, used only once at the very end; dropout randomly disables some neurons during training so the network spreads its learning across many units instead of leaning on a few, which usually improves generalization.

lessons.title: Convolutional and recurrent networks
lessons.grammar_note: Match the architecture to the data: convolutional networks suit grids such as images, while recurrent networks suit ordered sequences such as text or time series.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain why a plain fully connected network is a poor fit for images and sequences, and how two specialized designs fix that: convolutional neural networks for grid-like data such as images, and recurrent neural networks for ordered sequences such as text or sensor readings. Warm-up from the diagnostic: which type of network did we say suits images, and why? You will be able to describe, in plain terms, what a convolutional filter does as it slides across an image, why sharing those filter weights saves enormous numbers of parameters, and what pooling is for. You will also be able to explain how a recurrent network carries a hidden state forward through a sequence so that earlier items influence later ones, and why very long sequences strained the earliest recurrent designs. The aim is a solid mental picture of each architecture and a clear sense of when to reach for which, not a full mathematical treatment.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A full-size image fed into a fully connected layer would need one weight per pixel per neuron, which explodes immediately and ignores the fact that nearby pixels are related. A convolutional neural network, or CNN, instead slides small sets of shared weights, called filters, across the image. Each filter looks at a little local patch at a time and detects a pattern - an edge, a corner, a texture - anywhere it appears, because the same weights are reused at every position. Stacking convolutional layers lets early filters find simple patterns and later ones combine them into complex shapes, while pooling steps shrink the grid and keep the strongest responses, adding some tolerance to small shifts. A recurrent neural network, or RNN, handles ordered sequences by reading one item at a time and maintaining a hidden state that it updates at each step, so information from earlier items can flow to later ones. This makes RNNs natural for language and time series. Their weakness is reaching far back: plain RNNs struggle to connect distant items, which motivated gated variants and, eventually, the attention-based models of the next lesson.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: For a CNN, imagine a small 3 by 3 filter sliding over a photo. At each position it multiplies its nine weights by the nine pixels under it, sums the result, and writes one number into a feature map. Because the same nine weights are reused everywhere, a filter that learns to spot a vertical edge finds that edge in any corner of the image, and the layer needs only nine weights plus a bias rather than one weight per pixel. A real CNN stacks many such filters and layers, with pooling in between, and is the standard tool for photo classification and object detection. For an RNN, imagine processing the sentence 'the cat sat'. The network reads 'the', updates its hidden state, reads 'cat' while remembering 'the', updates again, then reads 'sat', so its final state reflects the whole phrase in order. This same loop handles stock prices, speech, and sensor streams. When sequences grow long, gated designs that learn what to keep and what to forget help the signal survive across many steps.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer and check yourself. 1) Why is a fully connected layer a poor fit for raw images? 2) What is a convolutional filter? 3) What does weight sharing in a CNN save? 4) What does pooling do? 5) What does a recurrent network carry forward through a sequence? 6) What is the main weakness of a plain RNN? Answers: 1) It needs one weight per pixel per neuron, which explodes in size and ignores that nearby pixels are related. 2) A small set of shared weights that slides across the input to detect a local pattern anywhere it appears. 3) A huge number of parameters, since the same filter weights are reused at every position. 4) It shrinks the grid and keeps the strongest responses, adding tolerance to small shifts. 5) A hidden state that is updated at each step so earlier items influence later ones. 6) It struggles to connect items that are far apart in a long sequence.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using a plain fully connected network on raw images and wondering why it needs so many parameters and generalizes poorly - convolution exists exactly to fix that. Mistake: thinking each position in a CNN has its own filter weights; the whole point is that the filter weights are shared across positions. Mistake: treating pooling as learning - it has no weights and only summarizes a region. Mistake: expecting a plain RNN to remember information from very far back, which is its known weak spot. Exit ticket: (a) Which architecture suits grid-like images, and which suits ordered sequences? (b) Why does weight sharing matter in a CNN? Answers: convolutional networks suit images while recurrent networks suit sequences; weight sharing lets one small filter detect a pattern anywhere in the input using very few parameters, which is both efficient and the reason CNNs generalize well on images.

lessons.title: Embeddings, transformers, and the practice of deep learning
lessons.grammar_note: An embedding turns a discrete item, such as a word, into a vector of numbers whose geometry captures meaning; attention then lets a model weigh which of those vectors matter.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain what an embedding is and why turning words into vectors of numbers is so useful, describe at a high level how the transformer architecture uses attention to relate every position in a sequence to every other, and list the practical realities of doing deep learning: data, compute, and frameworks. Warm-up from the diagnostic: the transformer relies mainly on which mechanism? You will also be able to name common applications of deep learning and, just as important, state several ethical considerations that come with deploying these systems. This is the course's wide-angle final reading, so the aim is informed fluency rather than deep math: you should leave able to say what a transformer does and why it replaced recurrent models for many sequence tasks, and able to talk sensibly about what it takes to build and responsibly deploy a deep learning system in the real world.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Computers cannot read words directly, so each word, or token, is first mapped to a vector of numbers called an embedding. These vectors are learned, and their geometry captures meaning: related words land near one another, and directions in the space can line up with real relationships. Transformers build on embeddings with a mechanism called attention. Instead of reading a sequence strictly left to right like a recurrent network, a transformer lets every position look at every other position at once and assign weights saying how relevant each is - so when processing 'it' in a sentence, the model can attend strongly to the noun it refers to, however far back that noun sits. Because this happens in parallel across the whole sequence and handles long-range links directly, transformers train efficiently on large data and have become the backbone of modern language and multimodal models. Stacking many attention layers, each refining the representations, is what gives large models their power. You do not need the full math to use the key idea: attention is a learned, weighted lookup across a sequence.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: Building a deep learning system comes down to three practical pillars. Data: you need enough relevant, reasonably clean examples, and how you collect, label, and split them often matters more than the exact architecture. Compute: training large networks takes specialized hardware such as graphics processors, and training cost in time, money, and energy grows fast with model and data size. Frameworks: libraries such as PyTorch and TensorFlow handle the heavy lifting - defining layers, running backpropagation automatically, and using the hardware - so you can focus on the model and data rather than low-level math. Applications span image recognition, speech transcription, machine translation, recommendation, drug discovery, and the large language models behind modern chat assistants. With that reach come real ethical considerations. Models can inherit and amplify bias present in their training data, leading to unfair outcomes. They can be hard to interpret, which complicates accountability when they are wrong. Training and data collection raise privacy and consent questions, and deployment raises concerns about misuse, environmental cost, and who is affected. Good practice treats these as first-class design constraints, not afterthoughts.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer and check yourself. 1) What is an embedding? 2) What mechanism is the transformer built around? 3) Give one advantage of attention over a plain recurrent network. 4) Name the three practical pillars of a deep learning project. 5) Name two frameworks used to build deep networks. 6) State one ethical consideration when deploying a deep learning system. Answers: 1) A learned vector of numbers that represents a discrete item such as a word, with related items placed near one another. 2) Attention, which weighs how relevant each position is to every other. 3) It can link distant items directly and process a whole sequence in parallel, rather than passing information step by step. 4) Data, compute, and frameworks. 5) PyTorch and TensorFlow. 6) Any of: inherited bias leading to unfair outcomes, poor interpretability, privacy and consent, misuse, or environmental cost.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking a transformer reads strictly left to right like a recurrent network; its attention relates all positions at once, which is its defining advantage. Mistake: treating embeddings as arbitrary codes rather than learned vectors whose geometry carries meaning. Mistake: believing architecture is everything while data quality is secondary - in practice, the data and how it is split usually decide the outcome. Mistake: treating ethical questions such as bias, privacy, and interpretability as afterthoughts instead of design constraints. Exit ticket: (a) In one sentence, what does attention let a model do? (b) Name one ethical consideration and one practical pillar of a deep learning project. Answers: attention lets each position in a sequence weigh how relevant every other position is and pull in the information it needs; an ethical consideration is that models can inherit and amplify bias in their data, and a practical pillar is data, compute, or frameworks.

items.translation: the part of machine learning that uses neural networks with many stacked layers to learn features from raw data
items.example: A photo classifier that learns edges, then shapes, then objects is deep learning at work.

items.translation: the basic unit of a network: it computes a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, then applies an activation
items.example: For inputs 4 and 1 with weights 0.5 and -1.0 and bias 0.2, the neuron's sum is z = 1.2.

items.translation: a nonlinear function applied to a neuron's weighted sum, without which stacked layers would collapse into one linear step
items.example: ReLU, relu(z) = max(0, z), is the most common hidden-layer activation.

items.translation: the adjustable numbers of a network: weights scale each input and the bias shifts the result
items.example: Training is the process of setting the weights and biases so the loss is small.

items.translation: a single number measuring how wrong the network's predictions are, which training tries to minimize
items.example: Mean squared error, L = (1/N) * sum((y_pred - y_true)^2), is a common regression loss.

items.translation: the update rule that steps weights opposite the gradient of the loss to make it smaller
items.example: With gradient +2.0 and learning rate 0.1, a weight of 0.8 becomes 0.8 - 0.1*2.0 = 0.6.

items.translation: applying the chain rule layer by layer, backward from the loss, to find each weight's gradient efficiently
items.example: Backpropagation supplies the gradients that gradient descent then uses on every step.

items.translation: fitting the training data so closely, including its noise, that the model fails on new data
items.example: 99 percent training accuracy but 70 percent validation accuracy is a classic sign of overfitting.

items.translation: the transformer mechanism that lets each position in a sequence weigh how relevant every other position is
items.example: Processing the word 'it', attention can focus on the noun it refers to, however far back it sits.
